# Education in Sweden
The Swedish education system is comprehensive and largely public, structured around a mandatory nine-year compulsory school (grundskola) from ages 6–7 to 15–16, which is divided into lower, middle, and upper stages. It emphasizes a national curriculum covering core subjects including Swedish, mathematics, physical education, English, sciences, social studies, and religion, with students starting to receive grades from year 6. National standardized tests occur in grades 3, 6, and 9. After compulsory schooling, students typically enter upper secondary school (gymnasieskola) for three years, choosing among 18 national preparatory and vocational programs, with a high enrollment rate (around 99%). Upper secondary education is course-based and finishes with a diploma project.
Higher education follows the Bologna system, with degrees at bachelor, master, and doctoral levels offered by universities and university colleges. Admission requires completion of upper secondary education or equivalent. The Swedish Scholastic Aptitude Test (SweSAT) serves as an additional admission tool. Higher education is mostly publicly funded; however, since 2011 tuition is free only for Swedish, EU/EEA, and Swiss citizens. Sweden also has a significant number of independent (free) schools funded by local municipalities, which must adhere to national curriculum and admission policies. Sweden’s education has internationally recognized standards but has seen fluctuations in PISA and PIRLS results, with immigrant influx cited as a challenge. The system also includes provisions for preschool, special education, and higher vocational training distinct from university degrees.
